elements.reason: The abstract explicitly labels the work as a "systematic-review and meta-analysis," identifying the report as a systematic review.

elements.quote: The objective of this systematic-review and meta-analysis was to compare the efficacy and safety of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis in hospitalized patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract states the main objective / review question directly.

elements.quote: MEDLINE and EMBASE were searched up to October 2021 for randomized clinical trials (RCTs) comparing high-dose with low-dose thromboprophylaxis in hospitalized adult patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies key inclusion criteria (RCTs, hospitalized adult COVID-19 patients, comparison of high- vs low-dose thromboprophylaxis) but does not state explicit exclusion criteria.

elements.quote: MEDLINE and EMBASE were searched up to October 2021 for randomized clinical trials (RCTs) comparing high-dose with low-dose thromboprophylaxis in hospitalized adult patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract names the information sources (MEDLINE and EMBASE) and specifies the date when they were last searched (up to October 2021).
The abstract does not describe the methods used to assess risk of bias in included studies; risk-of-bias assessment methods appear in the main text but are not reported in the abstract.
The abstract presents results (RRs, CIs, NNT) but does not describe the methods used to present and synthesize results (e.g., model or synthesis approach) within the abstract text.

elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies and participants and summarizes key study characteristics (critically ill vs non-critically ill trials).

elements.quote: VTE occurred in 2.9% of patients on high-dose and in 5.7% of patients on low-dose thromboprophylaxis (relative risk [RR] 0.53; 95% confidence intervals [CIs], 0.41-0.69; I 2 = 0%; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome, 22). Major bleeding occurred in 2.5% and 1.4% of patients, respectively (RR 1.78; 95% CI, 1.20-2.66; I 2 = 0%; number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome, 100). All-cause mortality did not differ between groups (RR 0.97; 95% CI, 0.75-1.26; I 2 = 47%).
elements.reason: The abstract reports results for the main outcomes (VTE, major bleeding, mortality) with event rates and effect estimates; although it does not give the number of studies per outcome, main outcome results and participant-level percentages are presented.

elements.quote: VTE occurred in 2.9% of patients on high-dose and in 5.7% of patients on low-dose thromboprophylaxis (relative risk [RR] 0.53; 95% confidence intervals [CIs], 0.41-0.69; I 2 = 0%; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome, 22).
elements.reason: A meta-analysis summary estimate (RR) and its 95% confidence interval are reported in the abstract.

elements.quote: In hospitalized patients with COVID-19, high-dose thromboprophylaxis is more effective than low-dose for the prevention of VTE but increases the risk of major bleeding.
elements.reason: The abstract compares groups, indicates direction of effect (high-dose more effective for VTE but increases bleeding) and which group is favored for each outcome.
The abstract does not include a brief summary of important limitations (risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision); limitations are discussed in the main text but are not reported in the abstract.

elements.quote: In hospitalized patients with COVID-19, high-dose thromboprophylaxis is more effective than low-dose for the prevention of VTE but increases the risk of major bleeding.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a concise interpretation of the results and their implications regarding efficacy and safety.
The abstract does not report the primary source of funding; although the main text notes there was no funding source, this information is not present in the abstract.
The abstract does not provide a registration name or registration number for the review.

elements.quote: The combination of systemic activation of coagulation, extensive pulmonary endotheliopathy and thromboinflammatory process caused by SARS-CoV2 results in an increased risk of thrombotic complications, mainly occurring in the venous system [1, 2]. In hospitalized COVID-19 patients, the incidence of venous thromboembolism (VTE) appears to be considerably higher compared to the incidence reported in medical patients with infection, sepsis or septic shock [3]. This risk increases with disease severity, with an estimated incidence of VTE of 17% in non-critically ill COVID-19 patients and 24% in those admitted to intensive care units (ICUs) [3]. ... Available data suggested that, despite pharmacologic thromboprophylaxis, there is a substantial residual risk of VTE and a non-negligible risk of bleeding events [3, 5]. In addition, it remains unclear whether prophylactic or higher doses of anticoagulants may reduce in-hospital mortality in COVID-19 patients [6, 7].
elements.reason: The introduction describes the current state (high VTE incidence, mechanisms, observational data) and highlights important uncertainties (residual VTE risk despite prophylaxis and unclear effects of higher doses).

elements.quote: Recent randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing the efficacy and safety of high-dose (i.e., intermediate or therapeutic dose) with low-dose thromboprophylaxis in patients hospitalised with COVID-19 reported conflicting findings [8-13]. Although the primary objectives of these studies were to evaluate whether high-dose anticoagulation may prevent COVID-19 progression to organ failure and death, most trials reported data on VTE and bleeding events. The objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the pooled efficacy and safety of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis for VTE in hospitalized patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The authors state that RCTs reported conflicting findings and explicitly state the objective and need to pool evidence to evaluate efficacy and safety, explaining the importance of the review.
No text in the provided evidence discusses existing similar systematic reviews, the need for the current review relative to prior reviews, or cites/frames this work as an update or replication.

elements.quote: The combination of systemic activation of coagulation, extensive pulmonary endotheliopathy and thromboinflammatory process caused by SARS-CoV2 results in an increased risk of thrombotic complications, mainly occurring in the venous system [1, 2].
elements.reason: While the disease mechanism is described, the manuscript does not provide a brief description of the proposed mechanism of action of the intervention (how anticoagulant doses specifically act) in the provided text.
The provided evidence contains no logic model or discussion presenting hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes for complex interventions or delivery contexts.

elements.quote: The objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the pooled efficacy and safety of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis for VTE in hospitalized patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The review objective is explicitly stated (evaluate pooled efficacy and safety of high- vs low-dose thromboprophylaxis for VTE in hospitalized COVID-19 patients). However, the statement is not presented using a structured question-formulation framework (e.g., explicit PICO phrasing), so it only partially meets the requirement to use a relevant question-formulation framework.

elements.quote: The objective of this systematic-review and meta-analysis was to compare the efficacy and safety of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis in hospitalized patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: For an intervention review, the planned comparison is clearly stated: population (hospitalized patients with COVID-19), intervention (high-dose thromboprophylaxis), comparator (low-dose thromboprophylaxis), and outcomes (efficacy and safety, with primary efficacy outcome VTE and primary safety outcome major bleeding described elsewhere in the text). This supplies the elements of a PICO-style comparison.

elements.quote: MEDLINE and EMBASE were searched from January 2020 up to October 2021 for RCTs comparing different regimens of venous thromboprophylaxis in hospitalized adult patients with COVID-19. ... RCTs including hospitalized patients with objectively diagnosed SARS-CoV2 infection and comparing high-dose anticoagulation (experimental group) with low-dose anticoagulation (control group) were eligible. Studies with a non-randomised design or published in languages other than English were excluded.
elements.reason: The eligibility criteria specify population (hospitalized adult patients with COVID-19), study design (RCTs), interventions (high- vs low-dose anticoagulation) and the search date range, but do not comprehensively report other study characteristics used for eligibility such as settings details, required follow-up duration, or all question-framework components.

elements.quote: MEDLINE and EMBASE were searched from January 2020 up to October 2021 for RCTs ... Studies with a non-randomised design or published in languages other than English were excluded.
elements.reason: The report specifies a date range (January 2020 to October 2021) and a language restriction (English), but does not state other report-characteristic restrictions such as publication or report status (e.g., unpublished, preprints) or additional dissemination criteria.
No information is provided distinguishing exclusion because outcomes were not measured from exclusion because outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: RCTs including hospitalized patients with objectively diagnosed SARS-CoV2 infection and comparing high-dose anticoagulation (experimental group) with low-dose anticoagulation (control group) were eligible. ... Sensitivity analyses were planned to compare the efficacy and safety of intermediate or therapeutic dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis, and of high-dose versus lowdose thromboprophylaxis in critically ill and non-critically ill COVID-19 patients. Critically ill patients included those admitted to ICU, patients requiring invasive mechanical ventilation, and patients with severe COVID-19 as defined by the study authors. All other patients were considered noncritically ill. We included a study in one of the subgroups above if more than 75% of patients in that study fulfilled these criteria.
elements.reason: The review explicitly defines the groups used for synthesis (high-dose vs low-dose; intermediate vs therapeutic; critically ill vs non-critically ill) and links subgroup grouping rules (including the >75% rule) to the comparisons in the review objectives.
No rationale is provided for notable eligibility restrictions (for example, no explanation is given for the language restriction or the chosen date range).

Secondary efficacy outcomes were all-cause mortality, acute myocardial infarction, acute ischemic stroke, acute peripheral arterial ischemic events, symptomatic or incidental deep vein thrombosis (DVT), and symptomatic or incidental pulmonary embolism (PE). The primary safety outcome was major bleeding as defined by the authors, while the secondary safety outcomes were clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

elements.quote: The pooled absolute risk reductions, number of patients needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) or for an additional harmful outcome (NNTH) with their CIs were calculated respectively for primary efficacy and safety outcomes in case of statistically significant findings.
elements.reason: The authors describe re-expressing synthesized relative effects as absolute risk reductions and NNT/NNTB/NNTH with CIs, i.e., methods to present results using another effect measure.
No justification for the choice of effect measure (e.g., rationale for using RR rather than odds ratio or risk difference) is provided in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: Two authors (EV and AP) independently screened the title and abstract of all records identified by the search. RCTs including hospitalized patients with objectively diagnosed SARS-CoV2 infection and comparing high-dose anticoagulation (experimental group) with low-dose anticoagulation (control group) were eligible. ... Sensitivity analyses were planned to compare the efficacy and safety of intermediate or therapeutic dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis, and of high-dose versus lowdose thromboprophylaxis in critically ill and non-critically ill COVID-19 patients. Critically ill patients included those admitted to ICU, patients requiring invasive mechanical ventilation, and patients with severe COVID-19 as defined by the study authors. All other patients were considered noncritically ill. We included a study in one of the subgroups above if more than 75% of patients in that study fulfilled these criteria.
elements.reason: The Methods section explicitly describes the screening process, the eligibility criteria for RCTs comparing high- versus low-dose anticoagulation, planned sensitivity/subgroup analyses (critically ill vs non-critically ill), and a rule (>75% threshold) for assigning studies to subgroups for synthesis.

elements.quote:
Categorical variables were described as counts and percentages and continuous variables presented as median (interquartile range) or mean (standard deviation), as appropriate. Pooled risk ratios (RRs) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and prediction intervals (PIs) were calculated using a random-effects model... The pooled absolute risk reductions, number of patients needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) or for an additional harmful outcome (NNTH) with their CIs were calculated respectively for primary efficacy and safety outcomes in case of statistically significant findings.

To help the interpretation of the data, we also expressed the results in absolute terms, i.e., the number of events that would occur in 1000 patients receiving high-dose thromboprophylaxis, using the observed risk in the low-dose group and the pooled relative risk with its 95% CIs. ... Statistical analyses were performed using R studio version 1.3.959, 'meta' and 'forest' packages [17].
elements.reason: The manuscript describes several data preparation and presentation methods (how categorical/continuous variables are summarized; use of random-effects model, RRs with CIs and PIs; calculation of pooled absolute risk reduction and NNTB/NNTH; conversion of pooled RR to events per 1000 using observed control risk). However, it does not explicitly describe methods for handling missing summary statistics or detailed data conversion procedures (e.g., imputation rules, transformation of medians to means, or methods used when studies lacked specific statistics), so the reporting is incomplete.

No methods text explicitly describes the tabular structures used to display results or the data included in those tables. While tables (Table 1, Table/Fig. layouts) are present in the results, the Methods do not describe how tables were constructed or which data fields were included.

elements.quote: "Gray squares indicate individual study estimates, whereas the gray horizontal lines indicate 95% confidence intervals of the individual studies. The diamond indicates the summary estimate with 95% confidence intervals. The horizontal black line refers to the prediction intervals which are displayed numerically under the 95% confidence intervals."
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly describes the graphical elements of the forest plot (symbols for individual studies, CIs, summary diamond, and prediction interval line) and also states in Methods that heterogeneity was evaluated by visual inspection of forest plots and publication bias by funnel plots.

elements.quote: "Critically ill patients included those admitted to ICU, patients requiring invasive mechanical ventilation, and patients with severe COVID-19 as defined by the study authors. All other patients were considered noncritically ill. We included a study in one of the subgroups above if more than 75% of patients in that study fulfil these criteria."

elements.quote: Over the last months, several studies showed that hospitalized patients with COVID-19 have a high risk of VTE despite receiving standard pharmacological thromboprophylaxis [3]. These observations raised the question of whether higher doses of anticoagulation could lower the thrombotic risk without compromising safety [3]. Observational studies reported promising results in terms of survival rate and respiratory failure reduction among patients receiving highdose anticoagulation, however, there was a concerning signal for an increased risk of bleeding complications [6, 7]. Based on these preliminary reports, international guidelines suggested, with a very low certainty, the administration of standard venous thromboprophylaxis in all COVID-19 hospitalized patients with consideration for higher doses in patients at higher risk of VTE [21-23]. The results of this metaanalysis support a greater efficacy from high-doses of thromboprophylaxis and suggest a better benefit-to-risk profile for therapeutic rather than intermediate doses.
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly places the study findings alongside other studies, observational reports, and international guideline recommendations, and states how the meta-analysis results relate to that existing evidence (supporting greater efficacy of high-dose prophylaxis and comparing benefit-to-risk).

elements.quote: There are some limitations which warrant discussion. First, the dose and duration of anticoagulant regimens varied widely across the studies. The sensitivity analysis including only RCTs in which patients received the intended high-dose or low-dose thromboprophylaxis yielded similar results compared to the primary analysis (Supplementary Figs. 13, 14). Furthermore, stratified analysis based on the use of intermediate- or therapeutic-dose thromboprophylaxis suggested a differential efficacy and larger effects with therapeutic-doses, in the absence of between-study heterogeneity. Second, the open-label design of all included trials represents a potential limitation and ascertainment bias cannot be excluded for VTE and major bleeding. Third, outcome definitions varied across trials, the occurrence of VTE during follow-up represented the primary efficacy outcome in only three RCTs, and all studies were underpowered to show differences in VTE or bleeding events. The relatively low incidence of VTE may be explained by the evaluation of symptomatic cases in the vast majority of the included RCTs and by the absence of protocol-mandated screening for VTE in the studies. Additional factors may include differences in study populations with inclusion of less severe cases or the effects of concomitant anti-inflammatory therapies on COVID-19-associated thrombo-inflammation [25]. The relatively low number of events may have prevented to show potentially relevant differences between intervention and control groups for the secondary outcomes. In addition, the low number of included studies limit the interpretation of all subgroup analyses which need to be interpreted with caution and regarded only as hypothesis generating. Fourth, the results of subgroup analysis on critically ill versus noncritically ill patients may be affected by the heterogeneous diagnostic criteria used for disease severity classification and by the inclusion of a mixed population in one RCT [20]. However, sensitivity analysis which considered only RCTs including critical patients yielded similar results for both VTE and major bleeding (Supplementary Figs. 15, 16).
elements.reason: The Discussion section explicitly states and details multiple limitations of the included evidence (heterogeneous dosing/duration, open-label designs/ascertainment bias, variable outcome definitions, underpowered studies/low event rates, few studies limiting subgroup analyses, and heterogeneous severity classification).
